pedagogy.summary: Children of 7-9 must distinguish two motions that are easy to conflate: Earth's daily SPIN on its axis (~24h, causing day and night) and its yearly ORBIT around the Sun (~365 days, one year). The load-bearing idea is that these are different motions on different timescales — the spin gives us day/night, the orbit gives us the year — and that day/night is NOT caused by the Sun moving or by clouds/switching off, but by us rotating into and out of sunlight. Teach it kinaesthetically first (child as Earth, lamp as Sun) then formalise with a globe, always naming which motion produces which effect and over what period.
bestPractices: Model it with the body and a lamp: a child holds a globe (or IS the Earth) beside a single fixed light source; slowly spinning shows a spot on the globe move from lit (day) into shadow (night) and back — one turn = one day. Walking the globe around the lamp while it keeps spinning shows the orbit = a year, making the two timescales concrete.

Separate the two motions explicitly before combining them: first master rotation → day/night alone, then add revolution → year. Keeping them apart initially prevents the classic conflation of 'a day' with 'a year'.

Anchor the effect to a familiar reference point — put a sticker on the child's home town on the globe and track when it is in daylight vs darkness as Earth turns, so day/night is felt as 'our side turning to face the Sun'.
Use a fixed, single light source and a darkened room so the lit/shadow boundary (the terminator) is sharp and the Sun is unmistakably NOT moving — the Earth is.
Attach numbers to the motions once the mechanism is felt: one spin ≈ 24 hours, one orbit ≈ 365 days, and connect 365 days to the calendar year the child already knows.
keyRepresentations: Globe + single fixed lamp (Sun) in a darkened room — the canonical model for day/night
Child's body as Earth spinning beside a lamp (kinaesthetic role-play)
Orbit path drawn on the floor with the Sun at the centre and Earth walked around it, one lap = one year
Coupled dual view: an external space view (Earth spinning beside the Sun) alongside a ground view (Sun appearing to rise/cross/set) so the child links the real spin to the apparent Sun movement
Terminator line (the day/night boundary) sweeping across a labelled globe
commonMisconceptions: Thinking day and night are caused by the Sun moving around a stationary Earth, or by the Sun switching off/being covered by clouds, rather than by Earth's rotation.
Confusing rotation with revolution — believing one spin takes a year, or that the orbit causes day and night.
Believing the Earth's orbit (distance from the Sun) causes day and night, or later, seasons — conflating the two motions and their effects.
Thinking the whole Earth is dark at night (not grasping that it is always daytime somewhere — the opposite side).
Assuming the Sun physically rises and sets by moving, not realising the apparent motion is produced by our own rotation.

learn.summary: Children aged 7-9 learn to distinguish two different motions of Earth on two different timescales: the daily SPIN on its axis (~24 hours, causing day and night) and the yearly ORBIT around the Sun (~365 days, one year). The load-bearing idea is that day/night is caused by us rotating into and out of sunlight, NOT by the Sun moving, switching off, or being covered by clouds. Teach kinaesthetically first (child or globe spinning beside a fixed lamp), separate the two motions before combining them, and always name which motion produces which effect over what period.

activities.title: Spin into night: the globe and the fixed lamp
feedback: If a learner says the Sun moved, point to the lamp: it has not changed position — only the globe turned. The Sun's apparent movement comes from our spin.
If a learner thinks the whole Earth is dark at night, rotate the globe to show the opposite side is lit — it is day there right now.
If a learner says the Sun went out or was covered, point out the lamp is still shining on the far side; night is just our side turned away.
activities.rationale: Day/night is fundamentally about motion; a familiar home-town anchor and a sharp terminator in a darkened room let children feel 'our side turning away from the Sun' rather than memorise a fact. The fixed lamp shows that Earth's spin alone is enough to produce day and night, matching what scientists know: Earth turns while the Sun does not circle it.
sourceClaims: UK National Curriculum Year 5 (Earth and space) requires pupils to 'use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky'.
Distinguishing rotation (day) from revolution (year) and using a lamp-and-globe model to make day/night concrete are standard recommendations for this age.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, set up a single fixed light source (a lamp) as the Sun; it must not move.
Hold or stand a globe beside the lamp and stick a marker on your home town.
Slowly spin the globe and watch your marked town travel from the lit side (day) into the shadow side (night) and back again — one full turn = one day.
Describe out loud what is moving: say whether the Sun or the globe is turning.
Find and point to the terminator — the sharp line where day meets night on the globe.
activities.intendedInsight: Day and night happen because Earth spins and our side turns to face or away from a Sun that stays put; it is always daytime somewhere on the other side.

activities.title: Two journeys, two clocks: separate spin from orbit
feedback: If a learner says one spin takes a year, slow down and separate the motions: a single turn is a day; the long walk around the Sun is the year.
If a learner attributes day/night to the orbit, return to the spin-only step — show day/night happening from turning in place, before any walking around.
Praise when a learner correctly labels each motion with its own effect and its own timescale.
activities.rationale: Mastering rotation alone before adding revolution prevents the classic conflation of 'a day' with 'a year'. Walking the orbit while spinning makes the two timescales concrete and keeps the cause of each effect distinct.
sourceClaims: Day and night arise from Earth's rotation, and one orbit of the Sun defines a year; children commonly hold the misconception that the Sun moves around the Earth.
Distinguishing rotation (day) from revolution (year) and using a lamp-and-globe model to make day/night concrete are standard recommendations for this age.
learnerActions: First, practise only the spin: turn the globe one full rotation and name it 'one day, about 24 hours'.
Next, draw an orbit path on the floor with the Sun (lamp) at the centre.

Keep the globe spinning while you walk it all the way around the Sun; one full lap = one year, about 365 days. Remember that the real Earth spins about 365 times during one lap, far more than you can turn the globe while walking.
Say aloud which motion gives day/night (the spin) and which gives the year (the orbit).
Connect 365 days to the calendar year you already know.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotation (spin) and revolution (orbit) are two different motions on two very different timescales: one spin makes a day, one orbit makes a year. The orbit does NOT cause day and night.

activities.title: Two views at once: the spin and the rising Sun
feedback: If a learner still says the Sun physically travels across the sky, pair the two views again so they see the same single motion two ways.

If a learner holds the Sun-circles-Earth model, let them act it out and notice it can also make the Sun seem to rise and set. Explain that both models match the ground view, but scientists have other evidence that Earth is the one spinning.
Reinforce when a learner explains sunrise/sunset as a result of Earth turning.
activities.rationale: Coupling an external space view with a ground view helps children connect the real rotation to the apparent movement of the Sun — the specific curriculum objective of explaining the Sun's apparent movement. Letting a learner act out the Sun-circles-Earth model shows that it produces the same sky view, so they see why the sky alone could not settle the question and why we rely on the scientific evidence that Earth spins.
sourceClaims: UK National Curriculum Year 5 (Earth and space) requires pupils to 'use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the sun across the sky'.
Day and night arise from Earth's rotation, and one orbit of the Sun defines a year; children commonly hold the misconception that the Sun moves around the Earth.
learnerActions: Watch, or model, the spinning Earth from the outside (a space view) at the same time as a ground view where the Sun appears to rise, cross the sky, and set.
As your home-town marker spins toward the light, notice the Sun 'rising'; as it spins away, notice the Sun 'setting'.
Say the click-moment aloud: 'It's not the Sun moving — it's me turning away from it.'

Test the old idea: try moving the Sun around a still Earth and notice that, from the ground, the Sun still seems to rise and set. Discuss how the spinning-Earth model gives the same sky, and that scientists know Earth really spins from other evidence, not from the sunrise view alone.
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun's apparent rise and set across the sky is produced by our own rotation; linking the real spin to the apparent Sun movement helps replace the geocentric intuition.

activities.title: Explore the lit hemisphere from any angle
feedback: If a learner thinks the whole planet is dark at night, have them view the opposite hemisphere and see it in daylight.
Confirm understanding when a learner can locate both a day region and a night region at the same moment.
activities.rationale: A free-orbit spatial view adds richness for grasping that it is always day somewhere, which counters the 'whole Earth is dark at night' misconception. The core spin-to-day, orbit-to-year insight can also be carried in a top-down or side view, so this spatial exploration is an enhancement rather than a requirement.
learnerActions: Using a 3D model or by moving around a spinning globe, view the lit hemisphere from different angles.
Fly or walk to the terminator and look along the day/night boundary.
Travel to the far (night) side and confirm it is dark while the near side is in day.
Explain why it is always day somewhere on Earth at the same time.
activities.intendedInsight: The Earth-Sun system is spatial: viewing the lit hemisphere from any angle makes it clear that day and night exist simultaneously on opposite sides of a spinning Earth.

activities.title: Check and sort: motion, effect, timescale
feedback: If a learner matches orbit to day/night, revisit the spin-only demonstration before re-sorting.
If a learner picks 'the Sun travels around Earth', return to the fixed-lamp model where the Sun never moves.
Encourage learners to say WHY, not just which answer, so you can hear which model they hold.
activities.rationale: Sorting causes, effects, and timescales and sequencing the parts of a day consolidate understanding. This checks recall and application after the mechanism is felt; used on its own it would test facts rather than build the motion intuition.
learnerActions: Match each motion to its effect and its timescale: spin → day/night → ~24 hours; orbit → year → ~365 days.
Put the parts of a day in order as a spot rotates through dawn, noon, dusk, and midnight.
Answer a question that confronts the 'Sun moves' idea by choosing and justifying what really happens.
Explain in your own words why the orbit does not cause day and night.
activities.intendedInsight: After building the motion intuition, learners can recall and apply the two facts and reject the common misconceptions.

constraints: Teach the spin before adding the orbit; combining them too early causes children to conflate 'a day' with 'a year'.
Use a single fixed light source in a darkened room so the terminator is sharp and the Sun is unmistakably NOT moving.
Attach numbers (one spin ≈ 24 hours, one orbit ≈ 365 days) only after the mechanism has been felt, and link 365 days to the calendar year the learner already knows.

A static labelled diagram (lit half, dark half, axis, orbit path) can name parts and serve as a reference or recap, but it cannot show the two motions unfolding over their different timescales; use it as consolidation, not the primary route.
A scored quiz or matching task checks recall and sorts causes/effects after understanding; on its own it does not build the motion intuition.
A free-orbit 3D view adds spatial richness (always day somewhere) but is not required; the spin-to-day, orbit-to-year insight can be carried in 2D with a top-down or side view.
Always name which motion produces which effect and over what period, so rotation and revolution stay distinct.

A role-play or dialogue can recount facts but does not by itself elicit the hands-on manipulation of the motion that makes spin and orbit concrete; pair any narration with actual manipulation of the model.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the source row (the NGSS claim and the general pedagogy-consensus claim); treat their support as unverified. Only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified:true.

The original row asserted that 'a static picture cannot disambiguate spin from orbit' and that a 2D interactive lets children 'feel' the timescales directly. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (static diagrams are useful for reference/recap; interactive or kinaesthetic motion makes timescales concrete).

The original row claimed a role-play/conversation 'cannot deliver the felt distinction' between spinning and orbiting. This has been softened to a scoped observable limit: narration alone does not elicit manipulation of the motion.

Activity 5 (check and sort) carries no sourceClaims: the cited claims support the facts and misconceptions being assessed (the topic), not the pedagogical principle that a sort consolidates or checks recall after understanding.

Timescale figures were checked: one rotation ≈ 24 hours (one day) and one orbit ≈ 365 days (one year) are correct as stated. The orbit causing the year (not day/night) and rotation causing day/night are internally consistent across the row.

An optional 'misconception-buster' toggle (trying the Sun-circles-Earth idea and finding it fails) is preserved as a learner-driven comparison, not as proof that one representation uniquely defeats the misconception.

probeDeeper: When you watch the Sun 'move' across the sky, what is really moving — the Sun or you?
How long does one spin take, and how long does one trip around the Sun take?
At night, has the Sun gone out, or is it still shining somewhere?
Which motion gives us a day, and which gives us a year?
assess.correctAnswer: Day and night happen because the Earth SPINS (rotates) on its axis once about every 24 hours. As it turns, the side facing the Sun has day and the side turned away has night. The Sun doesn't actually travel around us — it only LOOKS like it moves across the sky because we are the ones turning. Earth ALSO travels around the Sun, but that much slower journey takes a whole year (365 days) and gives us the year, not day and night.

errorPatterns.pattern: the Sun travels across and around the Earth to make day and night
errorPatterns.nextMove: Spin a globe beside a fixed lamp and 'ride' a figure on it — the child sees the lamp only APPEARS to move because the globe turns; the Sun stays put.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Sun travels all the way around the Earth once a day, and that gives us day and night.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child has the Sun doing the moving while Earth stays still

errorPatterns.pattern: day and night are caused by the Earth orbiting the Sun (once a day)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two motions explicitly: SPIN = one day (24h) causing day/night; ORBIT = one year (365 days) causing the year. Act both out.
errorPatterns.distractor: Day and night happen because the Earth travels all the way around the Sun each day.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child attributes day/night to Earth's yearly orbit, conflating rotation with revolution

errorPatterns.pattern: the Sun switches off, goes away, or is covered up at night
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Sun shines all the time; night is simply our part of Earth turned away from it — show with the globe that the far side is dark, not sunless.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child thinks the Sun stops shining or is hidden at night rather than our side turning away

responseLevels.gap: Says the Sun moves around Earth, or that Earth orbits the Sun each day to make day/night; no clear daily spin.
responseLevels.full: Explains day/night as Earth's ~24-hour spin (Sun only appears to move), distinguishes it from the ~365-day orbit that gives the year, and rejects the Sun-switching-off idea.
responseLevels.partial: Knows Earth spins to cause day/night OR knows it orbits yearly, but conflates the two motions or muddles their timescales.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: What makes it change from day to night and back again — is it the Sun travelling across and around the Earth, is it the Earth going all the way around the Sun each day, or is it something else? Tell me what really happens, and WHY it gives us day and night.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: This separates three common models: the Sun moving round Earth (geocentric), Earth orbiting the Sun once a day (rotation/revolution conflation), and the correct daily spin. Only a child who distinguishes the fast daily SPIN from the slow yearly ORBIT gets both the cause and the timescales right. The 'why' tier surfaces which model the child actually holds.
